svg.title: How the five stages became a sequence they were never meant to be. A vertical timeline. Events run from earliest at the top to latest at the bottom,.
svg.desc: A vertical timeline. Events run from earliest at the top to latest at the bottom, joined by a single vertical line. 6 events, in chronological order. Each has a date, a heading, and a short explanation to the right of the line. 1969: On Death and Dying is published. Elisabeth Kübler-Ross describes five responses she observed while interviewing people who were dying. The subject is a person facing their own death, not a person grieving someone else's. 1970s and 1980s: The model is borrowed for bereavement. It spreads into bereavement care, training and popular culture, applied to grieving a death rather than facing one. It is also flattened into five numbered steps along the way. 2005: Kübler-Ross says plainly that they are not a sequence. In On Grief and Grieving, written with David Kessler, she states the responses are not stops on a linear timeline, that not everyone experiences all of them, and that they can recur. 2000s onward: The evidence does not find a fixed order. Studies of bereaved people repeatedly fail to find everyone moving through a set sequence. The most common pattern reported is resilience rather than progression through stages. 2019: A sixth response is proposed. David Kessler adds finding meaning, arguing the original five stop at acceptance and leave out what people do afterwards. Now: The flattened version is still the one people arrive with. Most learners, and most families, meet grief as five stages in order. Expect to have to correct it, and expect a family to worry that someone is grieving wrongly because they are out of order.
svg.text: How the five stages became a sequence they were never meant to be
The model describes five responses. Almost everything that went wrong with it came from reading them as steps.
On Death and Dying is published
Elisabeth Kübler-Ross describes five responses she observed while interviewing people who were dying. The subject is a person facing their own
death, not a person grieving someone else's.
The model is borrowed for bereavement
It spreads into bereavement care, training and popular culture, applied to grieving a death rather than facing one. It is also flattened into five
numbered steps along the way.
Kübler-Ross says plainly that they are not a sequence
In On Grief and Grieving, written with David Kessler, she states the responses are not stops on a linear timeline, that not everyone experiences all
of them, and that they can recur.
2000s onward
The evidence does not find a fixed order
Studies of bereaved people repeatedly fail to find everyone moving through a set sequence. The most common pattern reported is resilience rather
than progression through stages.
A sixth response is proposed
David Kessler adds finding meaning, arguing the original five stop at acceptance and leave out what people do afterwards.
Now
The flattened version is still the one people arrive with
Most learners, and most families, meet grief as five stages in order. Expect to have to correct it, and expect a family to worry that someone is
grieving wrongly because they are out of order.
